utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I wonder before we continue with the witness if I could just raise two matters very briefly. The first has to do with scheduling and needs to be raised now. I -- this witness -- before -- before we started today, I asked, inquired of Defence counsel, as I often do, how long they expect the cross-examination to continue, information that we need for planning purposes for the next witnesses. I have to say I was quite surprised when I was told that they thought they would -- they indicated they would take the rest -- the entire day for cross-examination of the witness, and I raise the matter now because in our submission that's excessive given what this witness is all about. Now, I know that the witness has submitted an expert report so the length of the direct examination doesn't -- shouldn't limit the Defence because there's also the expert report to consider. The expert report, however, is only 18 pages long. It is what it is. It's mostly about victim impact, about -- some information about the scale of these events. The direct examination was 39 minutes. The cross-examination has already been 1 hour and 26 minutes. It seems to me that going the entire day today cross-examining this witness is just far in excess of what should be necessary for this kind of a witness given where we are already. We would ask respectfully that the Defence be instructed to finish its cross-examination no later than at the end of the second session, and that will then allow us to call further witnesses today. I'm also mindful of the schedule that the Court has imposed about finishing the trial, and we're trying to get our witnesses in here for testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On that point we've given you a day extra. You give us the 19th. We said you must finish on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Though I think whenever I give a date, an estimate, I think I always was careful to say that it could move a day or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're mindful of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In any event, I think with respect to this specific issue I've made my submission, and I think that -- I really think that the entire day for this witness is excessive for cross-examination, on top of an hour and 26 minutes which has already been done. And then I have a second matter to raise which is entirely separate and has to be raised in private session, so I don't know if the Court wants to deal with this matter first or would like me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friend indeed asked me how long my cross-examination would last, and I told him. It is true that we started our cross-examination yesterday. However, I don't believe that it is in dispute, and I believe that pursuant to the Trial Chamber's decision we already have this witness's testimony in the Babic case admitted in our file. He was examined-in-chief in detail in that other case. He wasn't examined by the Prosecutor in this case in great detail concerning all the details from his expert report. However, in the Babic case he gave a very detailed explanation of his report that's in the file, and I don't think the Prosecution should be bothered by the fact that the Defence wishes to cross-examine the witness a bit more extensively. It may go on for quite some time, but the Defence will keep in mind the need to deal with the matter expeditiously or with relevance and with concision. The sooner we complete the examination, the easier it will be for us to proceed. Now, my learned friend said that we should complete our cross-examination by the end of the next session. We will do our best to finish as soon as possible with regard to all the participants in the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Let me just make two short observations. One observation is that this particular witness is incomparable with other witnesses, precisely because he's a 92 bis witness and all the Prosecution did was just to touch on introductory remarks, hence only 39 minutes, and I don't think it would be fair to the Defence to try to limit them to that kind of period or something close to that period. I think they still have to go into substantive matters that the witness deals with, and I take into account the point raised by Mr. Milovancevic that the witness was extensively cross-examined in the Babic case, and they may want to ask questions on those issues. On the other hand, I would like to say, and that's the second point, that I welcome what you say, Mr. Milovancevic, that you will move with expedition and relevancy. Those are very important things. Please stay relevant. Now the Bench will certainly watch you like a hawk on that point. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic. Sorry. I beg your pardon, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Whiting had another point to raise. Yes, Mr. Whiting. Do you want to go into private session, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic, call your witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm sure having testified in this court before you do know what I'm going to tell you, but it's still my duty to remind you that you are bound today still by the declaration you made yesterday to tell the truth, nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am aware of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Loncar. We shall continue your cross-examination today. I have the same favour to ask of you today, which is to make sure that you make a slight pause before answering my question so that we facilitate the work of the interpreters today. Yesterday we completed one subject, which had to do with your stay at Begejci in 1991. We discussed whether it was a concentration camp or not, and you gave us your opinion thereof. I have one more question with regard to this. On all -- in all broadcasting companies, CNN, BBC, even the Croatian TV, or local TVs, we can see the Guantanamo prison which is surrounded by barbed wire, there are guards present with dogs, by judging the external appearance of the prison, would you deem it would be a concentration camp?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I comment by saying that the subject of my testimony is not Guantanamo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, I do agree with you that it is not. I merely wanted you to draw a comparison with what you described as the Begejci camp, and I wanted to establish whether you had any prejudice in regard to that. Let's move on. Did you write about your stay at Begejci, and did you identify the Begejci camp as the Serb collection centre or as a Serb collection camp or as a concentration camp?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a concentration camp, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with your CV, you gave us a very extensive presentation of your interventions and addresses at different conferences on several pages of your CV including the various subjects you dealt with. Among other things, in 1991, as the subject of presentation at conferences, that's page 2 of your CV, one of the topics you relate is the Chetniks and ethnic cleansing in Vojvodina which was published in Berlin, Germany, as far as I can conclude on the basis of this text. Do you as a psychiatrist believe to have the expertise necessary to deal with ethnic cleansing and violations of human rights?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I'd like a reference from my learned counsel as to which portion of the CV he's presumably quoting from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise if I wasn't precise. Mr. Loncar's CV, page 2. The title is "Presentations at seminars and conferences." Item number 1 or entry number 1 is the year 1992, and as far as I understood, this was work product by Mr. Loncar, ethnic cleansing and violation of human rights in Vojvodina. My question to him was whether he authored the presentation and whether he had the expertise necessary for it.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I already said, in any addition to the work I normally do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. The Prosecutor was on her feet before you can answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. But I thought I heard in the question of my learned colleague the term "Chetnik." But I don't see that either in the B/C/S or the English title in that entry for 1992, Berlin, Germany. Just let the record reflect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, your learned friend says the word "Chetnik" doesn't appear on that sentence. It is a question of characterisation of this witness's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no, I never mentioned that word. I was speaking of ethnic cleansing, and I never mentioned the term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me tell you what your question said, Mr. Milovancevic. "In connection with your CV you gave us a very extensive presentation of your interventions and addresses at various conferences on several pages of your CV including the various subjects you dealt with among other things in 1991 as the subject of presentation conferences, that's page 2 of your CV, one of the topics you relate is the Chetniks and ethnic cleansing in Vojvodina which was published in Berlin, Germany, as far as I can conclude on the basis of this text." So the word "Chetnik" in the transcript is there, and I don't want --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm grateful to my colleague for noticing that in the transcript. I wasn't following the transcript while I was putting questions, but I was literally quoting the title of the first "ouvre" as cited on this page, and -- and the word in the B/C/S was "etnicko," and perhaps that's why the interpreter may have misheard the term, but I never used the word in putting the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... used in terms of Chetnik and still gave us ethnic. We will take your word or give you the benefit of the doubt that you didn't use the word and you didn't intend using it. So will that make you happy? Is that okay, Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: There would be fine, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You. May proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to make one observation, Your Honours. I neither had the intention of using the word nor did I use it, because there was no context for me to use it. This is evidently misinterpretation, and I believe we have to clear up any doubts we have. Otherwise, it might be taken as my provocation of Mr. Loncar, and I don't see why that should be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, did you produce this work?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Beneath the year 1992, on page 2 of your CV there's the year 1993, and as one of your presentations given at various seminars and conferences is the topic "Mass-scale rape of women in the war against Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina." This was supposed to be given at a conference in 1993 in Opatija in Croatia. Is this article also your work product?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your CV under the year 1994, and that's the fourth date from the other one, the topic "Sexual violence against men in war," and you presented this topic in Dresden in Germany; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In 1998, which is on the following page, on page 3 of your CV, the fifth date from the top of the page, is your work dealing with the violations of the international humanitarian laws in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you presented that in Italy 1998, and that is again your work?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my presentation indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can accept, Mr. Milovancevic, that all those topics are his work, and you can avoid asking that question and move a little forward if you have any content -- subquestion to put to the witness, because I think now you're asking questions which are just delaying us. This is all his work. That's why he's written and said this is his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have mentioned those specific papers because I have singled them out from the rest of them because it seems to me that the topic that the expert has been dealing with is something that goes beyond his area of expertise, and that's why I'm going to put the following question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you an expert in international law? I have already asked you whether you have any legal knowledge. Do you believe that you have the ability to deal with the violations of international conventions and to deal with things that in their nature are of a legal substance? Could you answer that question, please, and tell me what you think about that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you allow me, I will answer this question in the following way: In my work I have not been dealing with legal matters. I have not dwelt upon legal norms. Second of all, the World Health Organisation has published a book in which it deals with the violation of human rights and the problem of health in people. Within the context of the World Health Organisation as the publisher of that book, I believe that -- I can say that this is an indicator of the doctor's right to deal with the issue of human rights, because human rights are not just a legal matter. It is something that everybody should be working towards improving, and everybody can do their bit in improving the state of human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, when you present your papers in your CV and when you say that there was a mass rape of women in the war against Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, this is the second paper on that list, could you please tell us who was it who waged this war against Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina? Was that a simultaneous war? Was it taking place at the same time? And who was -- who perpetrated all those rapes?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the perpetrator, in my research I have shown this, and the paper was published in an Assisi medical publication, as we will call it, which means that it was reviewed by two independent reviewers who we don't know who they are, and they approved of that paper, and in that paper I presented the research that I had carried out until then in the area of the raped women in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, I've asked this question because I personally believe that the subject that you're dealing with in this particular case is the status of victims of rape in the war. However, I am really curious about the title that you gave to your paper. I appreciate that you spoke to the victims. However, you qualified this act of rape as part of the war against Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Are you saying that this is part of the war?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a result of my research. Mass rapes were one of the means of waging this war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And this rape was used against the Bosnian and Croatian side. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you want to simplify all this, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this, I'll move on to your expert report. On the first page the title is "Medical centre for human rights." On the second page, and we're talking about the English version, page numbers 1 and 2, the second title is "Methodology of work with war victims," under II. And then on pages 2 and 3 of the English version, there is one segment of the text that I would like to speak about. The method of taking statements has several goals. The main ones are -- I hope that the Trial Chamber has been able to locate this part of the text in your expert report. You were talking about your research and about taking statements from victims. You say that you had two -- several goals and the main goal, and this can be found in the B/C/S version on the page ending with number 656, under 1, the main goal of taking statements was research of -- your research of international human rights conventions, and you're saying that the statement was done as a legal document. In this regard, I would like to know whether you as a psychiatrist spoke to your patients with a view to shaping their testimonials as legal documents.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, allow me to say something briefly in response to Mr. Milovancevic's question. On the previous page, in the document that I have before me, I showed the historical overview of all the testimonials and how data was collected. I can briefly repeat what the method of taking statements and testimonial is in order to be clear what we're talking about. And if the Trial Chamber will allow me to do this, I would like to provide a brief explanation. The method of taking testimonials dates back from the years '70, and it was initiated in Chile during the dictatorship when the first papers were published based on the data collected on traumas and the authors realised there was some therapeutical effect in doing that. From then onwards until this very day, and I can provide some references to the Trial Chamber, this method of taking testimonials has been used and such papers have been published in scientific papers in this area and in some other areas. Amongst other things, the method has been used in -- in the States by American experts on a group of refugees, and this is something that has been quoted in professional and scientific papers. Second of all, Your Honours, if I need to talk about psychological and therapeutical aspects of testimonial taking methods, I can say that this does indeed have a therapeutical effect. As for the legal shaping of documents I can provide a short explanation. A medical history taken for every patient that presents themselves in the hospital is an -- also an historical document and a legal document as well. The difference, if you want to simplify the matter, what is the difference between the method of testimonials and a patient history taken at the hospital. When a hospital -- when a patient presents themselves at the hospital, every doctor will start taking data on that patient, when his complaint started and how they developed. The only difference between the testimonial and the patient history is the fact that the testimonials are taken from victims. The principle is the same. You start talking to the victim. You start writing something together with the victim covering the period when the trauma started to the very end of that trauma. That is why -- that is why I said that the legal -- that the documents were shaped as legal documents because they have credibility in medicine, in our profession, as a medical documents that have to be a medical secret, and this is not me or anybody else playing prosecutors or judges or investigators. This is just for the victim to verbalise their traumatic experiences under safe circumstances and to go back to the reality of everyday life. Your Honours, what I can say based on my experience of working with the victims the first thing that you have to do is to write a testimonial, and I can say that I am proud of the fact that such patients were feeling better after providing those testimonials. None of them were angry. None of them felt the need to retaliate. They tried to re-socialise them, to give them back to the society and to restore their status, to remove the feeling of shame from them, and we gave them this impression that they were witnessing a certain period of history, and we tried to remove the feeling of shame that is very often present in the victims of rape, for example. And this is the first and the biggest success of this method. From that method we arrived at the documents that are historical documents, legal documents, if you will, and based on that we could see the intensity of the traumatic experience. We could assess how -- to what degree that person, that victim had to be -- had to undergo additional medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Loncar. You have provided a lot of detail about the essence of the testimonials that are taken from victims. With regard to your explanation given to the Trial Chamber, on page 1 of the English text there is a title "Testimonial or statement." This is in chapter 2, the methodology of work with war victims, and you've explained to us that one of the main goals was to take testimonials from the victims. Am I right in saying or in quoting a part of your expert report in which you say that the historical overview of the creation -- of a method for taking statement shows that this was as early as 1970s in Chile in order to help the victims of dictatorship, and the method of statement -- the essence of the method is a therapeutical goal?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The main goal of any statement taken is therapeutical effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If that is the main goal, the therapeutical effect that is, why do you say on the following page that the main method -- that the main goal of statement taking was research of violation of international human rights conventions and that therefore the statement was done as a legal document. If the main goal is therapy then this should be the main goal always?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I would just point out that I think this is the second time my learned friend characterises the first point under the list of methods as the main goal. In fact, the heading says the main ones are. So there is in fact -- there are several goals listed, and the one under the number 1 is just one of them, so I would not characterise that as the only goal. I would point that out. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with this remark put forward by my learned friend, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Under item 2 when you're talking about several main goals of the method of taking testimonials from victims, you say that by taking statements from victims you achieve a therapeutical effect. My question is relative to the rest of that sentence in which you say when you take a statement from a victim you turn the victim into a witness, which is the first step towards the person's reintegration into society. Is that a way to lift the burden from the victim's shoulder, and that's why the person came to you as a psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant was that this is a psychological condition that the victim changes. Not in legal terms but in psychological terms. When a victim provides their testimonial and when they go through this therapeutical procedure, in other words, when the victim tells a story to somebody, that person is no longer a victim. Not in legal terms but also becomes a witness which, in psychological terms, is much better for a victim. And I'm sure you will appreciate that as a lawyer, that nobody likes to be a victim. Nobody wants to be a victim with all the things that such a status brings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with these several main goals under point 3, you say that one of the main goals is to collect information for statistical studies and that these studies brought new insight into the use of torture as a weapon of war. Is that a correct understanding of what you wrote there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You go on to say under point 3 that the data collected showed or demonstrated the use of torture as a weapon of war to implement the strategy of ethnic cleansing. Is that a conclusion you arrived at as a psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I showed the causal link between the applied methods of torture and the strategy of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Ethnic cleansing is something that has to be established before this Tribunal or other courts of law. You instead take it as a matter of fact, or is it something that you yourself established?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, and I quote from the text, they pointed out cause and effect, let us say the causal link between the applied methods of torture and the strategy of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Under point 4, you state that the method of taking statements has several goals, among them the goal listed under point 4, which is classification of the types of torture with special emphasis on sexual abuse, both of women and men. Do you also believe sexual abuse to have been a weapon of war to further the strategy of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated in my report, I said that I established a causal link, a link of cause and effect between the applied methods of torture, including sexual abuse, and ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The method of statement-taking with these several goals you enumerated, did it apply to the territory of the then SAO Krajina or the RSK, although this area was under the protection of the United Nations' forces or, as they were called, the UNPAs?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will reply by saying that we worked with those victims that we were able to get in touch with, all of those victims that approached us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The victims hailed from which areas?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were from the territory of the Republic of Croatia. These persons were displaced because they were driven away, and there were persons from Bosnia-Herzegovina who were refugees, who had fled the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since you are now presenting your expertise in the Martic case, are these four goals or the information you conveyed to us relative to or are -- do they apply to the areas listed in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report applies to the UNPA areas, that is to say the areas under the control of Serbian forces. The persons involved were persons who were expelled from the area and whom we were able to make contact with and talk to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: To clarify the matter completely, on the basis of your conversations with persons from these areas, you arrived at the conclusion in this expert report of yours that torture, methods of torture applied in the war were directly connected with the strategies of ethnic cleansing that were being implemented there, and you place special emphasis on the sexual abuse of both women and men as a strategy or as a weapon of war and part of this strategy of ethnic cleansing. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please have Prosecution 65 ter document number 327 on our screens. That is the UNCIVPOL report for Sector South. Before the document comes up on our screens, and that's document 327 from the 65 ter list, this is a document by the UNCIVPOL which contains a summary overview of crimes committed against members of the Croatian community in Sector South over a longer period of time. I will refer you to one portion of the document. I believe we are seeing the text of the document on the screen. Yes, that's correct. That's the document. Mr. Loncar, you have before you a document by the United Nations, UNPROFOR, sent by John McElligott to Mr. Thornberry. Apologies. The document is dated 27 July 1993, and the subject is "Crimes complimented against Croats in Sector South." Could we please look at page 3 of the document. Yes, could we have the whole table blown up, please. Mr. Loncar, you see here a list of crimes recorded by UNPROFOR over a long period of time. For instance, we have August 1992 and May 1993. So that's the period. Now, entry 29 lists all -- or, rather, the second column shows all sorts of crime, arson, assault, all the way to even murder. We already discussed this. But please look at entry number 20, which says "Rape." Now, you see that throughout the period between August 1992 and May 1993, the population reporting forest arson, theft of flour sacks and so on and so forth, there were different types of crime, but not a single one of them reported rape as a crime. At least it wasn't recorded by UNPROFOR. And do you see that on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just -- I think I object -- I object to this question. The witness has testified that the victims were from the territory of Croatia, and there were others of course from Bosnia-Herzegovina, but these are the territories to which he referred. Now, this report is from Sector South. This is quite a different geographic scope from the territories described by the witness. I'm not -- I disagree with this line of questioning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in answering my questions, Mr. Loncar said that sexual abuse as a weapon of war also applied to the UNPAs. I'm now presenting him with a report covering one such area, a very large one, where some -- a range of some 20 crimes were reported, and I don't see why my learned friend should object to that. This is a relevant matter. Between August of one year and the May of the next year not a single incidence of rape was reported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Doctor, did you do any research in this area that's being shown on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. By your leave, I shall try to answer the question by giving you some facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to know if you did research here. And did you do your research in collaboration with the people who compiled this report that's on the screen? Did you work hand-in-hand with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sector South covers the Knin area, if I'm well aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you work with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I do know from my work with victims, there was sexual abuse precisely in the Knin camps. And I'm not surprised that UNCIVPOL was unable to get hold of such information, because I suspect that victims of such crimes were not within UNCIVPOL's reach. That's the first part of my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Just before you go to your second part, are you able to answer my question with a simple yes or no: Did you work in collaboration with the people who --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In that event, then, your question's become irrelevant -- I beg your pardon, disallowed, Mr. Milovancevic. Put it this way, let me rephrase, the objection is upheld. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please look at the next page of the document. Could you please blow up the text a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, we were looking at this other page where I wasn't allowed to put a question to you. We saw that the report was relative to Vrlika, Drnis, Bratiskovci, Smokovic, Medak, Teslingard, Zaluznica, Knin, Kistanja, Benkovac, Obrovac, Gracac, Donji Lapac, and Korenica. Not just Knin. Did you work with victims from these areas?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I said Knin I meant what we normally call UNPA south, and based on the document I saw a moment ago, in addition to the numbers of people who reported such incidences of crimes, I repeat that I'm not surprised that no incidence of sexual abuse was reported on, and I say that for the following reasons: As we know on the basis of our medical statistics, only 1 in 5 or 1 out of 6 rape incidences would be reported in peacetime. One can well expect that in wartime, and especially in the circumstances of being held in prison or in a camp, the numbers of reported incidences of rape should be even lower. And I would like to finish off by saying that the figure that Mr. Milovancevic referred us to under 20 where there are no cases of rape reported is something that does not come as a surprise to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It comes as a surprise to me that UNCIVPOL, who registered every single crime from petty theft to any other, that he would not report on this. But there was one witness, a lady, who testified before the Tribunal, whose husband and father had been killed. In answering the question put by the Defence as to whether she had heard of rape in her area, she responded -- in Saborsko, she said, "Well, there were all sorts of crime but not that of rape." Do you have any information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear any such thing from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is enough. Witness, we are going to move on to another topic. In answering the Prosecutor's question, you said that you were arrested in 1993. Actually, that you were brought to the police station on the pretext that you had to change your ID. Who was who arrested you? Whose authorities?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've already answered that question. I was brought in for an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who was it who brought you in?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian police brought you in for an interview? You explained that this was supposedly because your ID was not in order, but the matter of the fact was the nature of your work, i.e., your research of crime. You only talk about crimes committed against the Croats. Why would then the Croat authorities bring you in? Why would they be bothered by that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speculate what bothered whom. That -- that time I did what I did, what I'm talking about today. And as you yourself have asked me, and you have alleged that my work is some sort of a quasi-prosecution, I suppose, but I can only suppose that out of ignorance or out of I don't know what the Croatian authorities had doubts about my work, just like you do here. And as for the victims themselves, I worked with everybody regardless of their religion or ethnic background because I believe that being a victim is a universal thing. I also believe that perpetrators have to be punished regardless of their religious or ethnic affiliation and that they should be named.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the English version of your expert report, on page 1, under II, we have the following title, "Methodology of work with war victims," and in B/C/S the page is 655. Have you been able to locate that part of the text?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And you -- you explain in this part, in the first paragraph, that the medical centre for human rights in its work with victims of aggression against Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina used several methods of data collection. With regard to this term "aggression against Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina," could you please tell us who the aggressor was? What period of time was that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did that between 1991 and 1995. When I used the term "aggression," that's the period of time that I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with that qualification, the work with victims of aggression against Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, you portray Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina as those who suffered aggression. Who was the aggressor in your view?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when we're talking about the aggression and the aggressor, this is a notorious fact. If I say that somebody attacked Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, it has to be somebody from the outside, and it is a notorious fact who attacked those two countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really curious to hear it from you who it was if you say that it is a notorious fact. I would like to hear this from you.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this goes beyond the scope of my expert report on the victims of war. I have my personal opinion that I can share with you if that is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, you provided an expert report which was admitted as evidence in another case, and based on your opinion a valid sentence was passed, and here another person is being tried based on your expert report in which you say that you used the methodology of work with victims of war, which was based on the collection of data from war victims of aggression against Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. If you wrote this in your report, I expect from you not to avoid providing me an answer.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can provide you any answers about victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe this is a convenient moment for our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed, Mr. Milovancevic. We will take a short break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, the OTP has provided us with a statement that you gave to the OTP. This is part of the disclosed material. And with it has provided us with a set of colour photos. I have those documents only in this form. I would kindly ask the usher to display these photos on the screen. Those photos are closely connected with the topic that we were discussing, that is developments during the war and the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if we could see these photos displayed on the ELMO, if you will allow this, Your Honour. You can display one by one photo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before the photographs are displayed, can we hear what Ms. Valabhji has got to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm just wondering what the relevance of this is. Yesterday my learned colleague touched very briefly on the subject of this statement given in October 2005, and it concerns areas that are simply not relevant to this indictment. I believe those areas are in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So my first objection is on the grounds of relevance. And second, Your Honour, I think now we are probably going beyond the scope of the expert's evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Naturally, the Bench doesn't know what those pictures are all about. Mr. Milovancevic, there is an objection raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the intention of the Defence counsel is to present these photos, which are photos of victims of whom this witness has direct knowledge in order to check the objectivity of the witness and to check his words in chapter II on methodology of work with war victims, that he spoke with victims of aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia. In other words, from the very beginning of his work the witness started from a fact that the situation was what it was, which the Defence wants to challenge and prove that this was indeed not the fact. We are trying to test the credibility of the witness that we have here today, and this is the idea behind the intention to show the photos to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do the photos relate to the report that the witness has filed in this case? Are they about the victims that he says he interviewed relating to this specific case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are photos of victims from Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The photos are relative to the persons, i.e., victims of whom the expert has direct knowledge and of whom he spoke before this Tribunal in a different case. These photos were provided to us by the OTP as accompanying material. With this regard, we would like to put questions to the witness in order to test his way of thinking while dealing with the subject. In other words, we want to see what his approach was to the matter at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were these accompanying material to the report that this witness gave in this matter or accompanying material in which case? I notice you, Ms. Valabhji, but I just want to get an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if your question was put to you, I would like to say that this is part of the material that has been provided to us by the OTP in connection with the expert report of this witness, and any material provided to us in connection with this witness is relevant, in our view. This is part of the material that has been provided to us with the OTP. The material is relevant to victims, the victims of war in Croatia and in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think there might be some misunderstanding on the part of my learned colleague as to the disclosure that took place with regard to this particular witness statement. Under Rule 66 of the Rules, witness statements of witnesses who testify here are required to be disclosed, and I believe the disclosure took place under this Rule. So I'm not really sure about the characterisation of this accompanying material or material that is provided in connection with the expert report, which is how my learned colleague identified it. It's simply Rule 66 disclosure, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in terms of Rule 66, you disclosed this material to the Defence in this case?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The objection is overruled. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can we have the first photo on the ELMO, Mr. Usher, in the same order you have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you would know better, is this something that we must -- that we need to go into private session about, or is it something that we can do in open session, what we are about to do now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no need for private session, Your Honour. There is no ID material in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photo, Mr. Loncar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it yet on the ELMO, if I'm supposed to see it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It should be on the ELMO. If not, then you can look at the photo next to you.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I recognise this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where does this photo originate from and what does it represent?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It represents victims from Doljani, the year is 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The victim is who, of what ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I had the photo on the screen just briefly and now it has disappeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. We now have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Doljani is in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this is a Croatian victim, and the victim is a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And he was victimised by Muslims? The interpreter's apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the next photo, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The answer was "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this photo you can see the lorry that transported those Croatian victims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we display the next photo, please. A number of victims are seen here, and we can see people working around them in order to identify them. Am I right, sir?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this was a doctor affiliated with UNPROFOR, if my memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Again, these are Croatian victims who suffered at the hands of the Muslim forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we move on to the next photo, please. What is the characteristic of this victim in the photo? Can you recognise anything?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's very hard for me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does that person have burns?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would say that, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And this is a Croat again?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we move on? Next photo, please. What is the hand in the white glove pointing to? I suppose it is pointing to the injuries on the skins of victim?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. I could agree with you, although I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we move on and show the next photo? Here we can see a victim in civilian clothes, I believe. And those are all victims from -- from one location?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The village is Doljani, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is a village where the Croatian population suffered at the hands of the Muslim forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we move on? The next photo, please. Another victim that was found there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Move on. Another photo of those victims from Doljani?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Move on. What can you tell us about the upper body of this victim? Can you tell us from the photo?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first victim?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the first victim.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the front of the photo. This one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to say. I must -- I must admit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the victim's head? Can you see whether the head is there or not? Is it clear from the photo?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we move on? Next photo, please. In this photo you can see a victim whose legs are closer to us, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Another victim from Doljani?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In uniform or in civilian clothes; can you tell?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the person is wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we go on, please? Another victim from Doljani, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Move on, please. This is a photo depicting the lorry in which the victims were brought to the place of the examination?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we move on? The same lorry, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Move on. A different angle, the same lorry?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. This victim suffered head injuries, as far as you can tell?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Move on, please. Thank you. Move on, please. This one is not very clear. It shows a person manipulating another person or a victim. This is the same lorry, and a victim is being removed from the lorry?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we go on? This is the room to which these two lorries carrying victims bodies were brought to. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we move on, please? Thank you. Under the clothes of the victim, you can see abdominal injuries and also head injuries?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell something about the nature of these wounds, how they were inflicted?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the photo, I suppose that those were firearm wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we move on? Thank you. There is just a few more. We'll be over soon. These are all the victims in a photo.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I believe that this was the last photo. I would like to thank the usher for helping us. These photos were shown to you, Mr. Loncar, because I wanted to ask you this: Do they show that in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993 there was an armed conflict in which the Muslim forces created so many and such victims on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour. I object. What is the relevance of this line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's -- what is the relevance of this line of questioning, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the relevance lies in the very first sentence of the second chapter of the expert report, on page 1 in the English version, titled "Methodology of work with war victims." The point of departure of this expert witness is that these were victims of aggression on Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The photographs show that in this specific case there was a Muslim attack on Croat civilian population and members of armed forces. The assertion contained in this first sentence that what was the case was in fact an aggression by Serbs against Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina is something that directly affects one's reasoning and conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you just read again that very sentence on which you say the relevance is based? I didn't hear you mention the word "Serbian" when you read that sentence. You said to us the point of departure of this expert witness is that the photographs show that in this specific case there was -- I beg your pardon, that these were victims of aggression on Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Full stop. That's where you stopped. You didn't mention Serbs. And right through your showing these photographs, you were telling the witness that these -- the ethnicity of these people and where they came from, that they came from Doljani. I have questions to ask him about those questions that you put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in his report, the expert speaks of an aggression on Croatia and Croats and on Bosnia and Herzegovina and on Bosniak Muslim population carried out by a third party. Now, based on these photographs, we came to the conclusion that in Bosnia where Croats, Muslims and Serbs lived, in this particular case it was the Muslim forces who massacred Croatian population. Now, I wanted to ask the expert to explain to us who the aggressor was and who the victims were and what was involved there. I'm simply trying to verify this expert's point of departure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, Mr. Milovancevic, has this witness said in his report who the aggressor was? You know, these photographs that you have shown us, I don't know what time they relate to. I don't know how this witness determines the ethnicity of these people by looking at the photographs, and how he determines where they come from other than that you told him who they were and where they came from and he just agreed with you. And if that first sentence is anything to go by, he says it's an aggression perpetrated on Croats and Bosnia and Herzegovinian people. He hasn't sort of indicated by who. And remember, the purpose for this witness's testimony, it's not -- he's not giving factual evidence. He's giving expert opinion evidence on the effects of trauma. Now you want him to be an eyewitness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- no, Your Honour. No. To my direct question as to who committed the aggression the witness answered that this was a notorious fact. Since to me this is not a notorious fact, I had to present him with material that he himself submitted to the Prosecution, where he spoke of Croat victims suffering at the hands of the Muslim armed forces. The entire expert report, Your Honour, and we can see that in the next chapter, that there was a cause and effect link between methods of torture and the strategy of ethnic cleansing. This entire report is talking about the Serb joint criminal enterprise, and the Prosecutor is trying to establish this through the report. And what I'm asking is whether this witness has the minimum required level of objectivity and impartiality in establishing facts and drawing conclusions. If in his first sentence of the report he states that this was an aggression against Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and he refuses to answer my question as to who committed the aggression, he simply answers by saying, "Well, it is a well known fact," I had to refer him to a specific case and ask him, well, who the perpetrator in this particular case was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But for him to be able to answer you yes or no on that question, he must be able to tell us whether he witnessed the aggression perpetrated on these people shown on the picture. Not as an expert but as an eyewitness. He must be able to tell us that he saw it happen; otherwise he can't tell us who perpetrated the aggression on those people, can he? And the sentence in his report that you referred us to does not mention any aggressor. Now, you've got to tell this Bench the link that you establish between his report and these photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have so far been discussing the objection by the Prosecution as to the relevance of my questions to this witness. We have not arrived at the answers to the questions that -- the one that you have just touched upon. We were just about to receive these answers from the witness. We don't know them as yet. In our discussion, we have gone ahead of us. At least that's the way I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe you went ahead of yourself by showing these photographs before you established the basis for showing them. You were allowed to show those photographs because you said they were disclosed to you by the OTP, but you don't seem to have established any basis. If you had established a basis by the time you showed those photographs, we would have understood where you were going. We didn't understand where you were going. I still don't understand where you are going. And it's a basic rule of prosecution that you've got to lay a foundation for whatever exhibit you'd like to tender in court. So if you give us exhibits for which you have laid no foundation, obviously they cannot be accepted until and unless you establish the basis for their coming in, and you can't tell us, can't tell the Court, that we have run ahead of ourselves. You are in control of the proceedings at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully agree with what you've just said. I withdraw what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then if you do want to ask this witness questions relating to those photographs, lay the foundation, because you just sprung photographs on us. We don't know where they come from, what the -- what the basis of producing them is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, I will do so and very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, on the 25th and 26th of October --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, just for the record, in this respect then the objection is upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you give a statement to the OTP on the 25th and 26th of October, 2005 concerning the victims in this particular village that we have just looked at?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be frank and tell you that I contacted the Prosecution on several occasions. I don't recall the dates. That is why I cannot recall that specific document, but I do trust the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The OTP gave the Defence your statement given on the 25th and 26th of October, 2005 in the B/C/S version, where in 38 paragraphs you -- interpreter's correction, in 28 paragraphs you speak of the massacre committed on the Croat population in Doljani, 1993. Do you agree that that is indeed the case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the document with me, but I do know that I gave a statement. I just can't be sure about the document. I don't have it here with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke of the work of the centre, that is to say the medical centre for human rights, and in paragraph 12 of your statement you say that all the investigations are well documented in archives in the centre. You say that the bodies were brought over from Doljani where you, together with your colleague Marko Rados and a British doctor from UNPROFOR's British contingent, examined the dead bodies. Since it was apparently a case of war crimes, that is why UNPROFOR was associated. That's at paragraph 18. And then at paragraph 20, you say, "I'm handing over a report titled 'Report on the massacre in Doljani near Jablanica,' dated 4 August 1993 in Medjugorje." I'm sorry, I've been speeding. Therefore, you state in paragraph 20 that you were handing over a report titled "Report on the massacre in Doljani near Jablanica," dated 4 August 1993, and a subsequent investigative report titled "Report on the Muslim crimes in Doljani village, Jablanica municipality." And then you go on to explain the photographs that I just showed you. The photographs are part of your statement, and my questions had to do with them. Do you remember the context of the statement, of the photographs, and the event itself?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that I reported on the massacre together with my colleagues, but I find it difficult to speak of the specific document because I don't have it with me here. Is this document a report by the centre? Is it a testimonial or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, I apologise for interrupting you. The point of my question was not to try and force you to recall a document without giving it to you. I admit that it is difficult. My question to you in connection with it was who was the aggressor who committed this crime on the Croat population?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That question has been ruled out of order until you have laid a basis for it. Just lay a basis. You said you were going to do so in five minutes or in a short while. I said to you this witness is not an eyewitness. The part of the report that you quoted to this Court which you say you rely on to suggest that somebody else, a third party attacked these people doesn't mention the name of the aggressor. He just said aggression on Croats and Bosniaks. He doesn't say who the aggressor is. And he's not an eyewitness. He didn't witness the massacre. He's dealing with post-traumatic stress situations, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only thought of the fact that the OTP provided us with the statement that the person -- the witness himself was involved being there on the spot when the victims were brought over by UNPROFOR, and that the victims suffered at the hands of Muslim armed forces. I merely wanted to hear from the witness whether he had heard of that. Of course, I did not mean to imply that he was an eyewitness, that he was there witnessing the massacre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, now I don't understand what you're saying. You want to -- why can't you get that answer from other witnesses? This witness has told us what he told us in his report. If you can refer me to his report where he says that these victims were attacked by a particular third party, then you can put your question, and in fact your question would be redundant because the answer will be in the statement itself, the written statement itself. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will finish with this topic, but I don't want to leave the situation unclear. What I had in mind was the document given by the OTP, which was the statement by Mladen Loncar, the witness present here, which was taken by the OTP on the 25th and 26th of October, 2005, where in paragraph 20 this witness states, and I quote: "I'm handing over a report," he says to the OTP, "titled report on the massacre at Doljani near Jablanica," dated the 4th of August, 1993, as well as a subsequent investigating report titled 'report on the Muslim crimes in Doljani village, Jablanica municipality.'" This is verbatim what the witness stated in his statement for the OTP, and my question to him was whether these photographs had anything to do with his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just let me read you what you have just quoted. You say: "I am handing over a report," he says to the OTP, "titled 'report on the massacre at Doljani near Jablanica dated the 4th of August, 1993, as well as a subsequent report entitled 'report on the Muslim crimes.'" So the criminals here are Muslims. He tells you. He's given you the answer there. Muslim crimes. I'm quoting what you have just quoted to us. In Doljani village. So it looks like the criminals were the Muslims in this report that he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. And this is precisely the answer that I wanted to get from the witness, whether he said that in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, now you've got it. You've found it yourself in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: My next question for the witness: Does the witness know that the six persons from Bosnia and Herzegovina, from the Croatian leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Jadranko Prlic and others, are being tried at this Tribunal for the crimes committed by the armed forces of Croatia against the Muslim population? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the relevance of that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance is in the fact that the witness has been talking about the Serbian aggression in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina all this time, and the essence of his finding that we have before us is the fact that the Serbs launched the aggression and committed all the crimes in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, you have not referred this Court to a Serbian -- to an allegation by this witness against Serbs, and you are now saying that there are -- he's making allegations against Serbs. We have just established through your own effort that he says it is Muslim crimes in Doljani, whatever that place is called, and I do not now understand why you're asking the question that you're asking, and I don't see the relevance of that question, to ask him about people who are being tried before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Your Honour, if the Muslim forces in this specific village, in Doljani, committed this crime against Croats was said by the witness in another case, and in yet another case it is being tried that Croats committed crimes against the Muslims, and the witness knows it all too well. But in his finding, in his report, he only speaks about the Serbian aggression, and this is his starting point. This is a condition sine qua non. Let us first establish that and then we will go on to more specific things. And this is the essence of my cross-examination of this witness. This is what I'm trying to check with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you are perfectly entitled to ask if I question to this witness provided that the question is relevant, and if it is not relevant, I'm afraid the Chamber cannot allow it. You have not established the relevance of the question you've just put about other people who are being tried in this Tribunal. It has nothing to do with this witness's report, and that question will not be allowed until and unless you establish the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, you were an expert witness in the trial against Mr. Babic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: During that trial the OTP examined you about the report that we have before you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: During that trial, during the Babic case, Mr. Babic's Defence did not cross-examine you. They did not have a single question for you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they did have some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can I now ask the usher to distribute the transcript from the Babic case. We have ample number of copies for all the participants in the trial as well as for the interpreters. Before you, Mr. Loncar, as well as before all the others in the courtroom, you have the transcript from the trial on the 1st of April, 2004, in the Babic case. In connection with this -- just bear with me for a moment, please. If you look at page 70 of the transcript, and the transcript starts with page 66, you will see that Mr. Whiting starts his introduction on page 70. Mr. Whiting says that he will take -- that he will make the brief opening remarks, and then he will examine the witness, and he only has one witness, Mr. Mladen Loncar. Do you agree with that? This is on page 70. You will find the number in the top right-hand corner. In the first third of the text --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The only thing that is wrong here, and it is an error in the transcript, your name is written incorrectly. On pages 71, 72, and 73, Mr. Whiting talks about the agreement that has been reached with Mr. Babic, and on page 74, Mr. Whiting refers to the statement of the first witness. This is at the bottom of page 74, and it starts with line 21, and in that part of the transcript Mr. Whiting informs the Trial Chamber that a witness from Dubica describes how many Croats fled his village, the village of Dubica, during the conflict and that on the 20th of October, 1991, 53 civilians were killed. Those were accommodated in the local fire station where they were guarded by the local Serbs and the JNA. When you drafted your expert report, did -- is this something that you came by?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to compare the data, whether they concur. Can the counsel repeat his question, please, Your Honours? I found everything in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Loncar. It is very difficult to find things in the transcript. On page 74, line 21, Mr. Whiting speaks about a witness from Dubica who describes how many Croats fled the village of Dubica during the conflict and that on the 20th of October, 53 civilians were accommodated in the fire station where they were guarded by local Serbs and the JNA. Is this what is -- what you found?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Fifty-three civilians in the village of Dubica who were detained in the local fire station. This is what I found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 76 of this transcript, line 8 of the transcript, Mr. Whiting quotes a second witness. This is on page 76, if you can find this for me, please. Line 8. And he says here a second witness provides records about the attack by Serb forces on Skabrnja. A second witness provides evidence about the attack by Serb forces on Skabrnja on the 18th November 1991. Mr. Whiting goes on to say this witness tells how Serb soldiers, including JNA soldiers and SAO Krajina soldiers, intentionally, deliberately executed civilians during the attack, including elderly and women. Is this information that concurs with what you state in your expert report based on your research?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What does he state in his expert report? Mr. Milovancevic, what does he state in his expert report that he's supposed to concur with this? You're telling him what Mr. Whiting told him. You're not telling him what he said. You see, you're seeking -- you're seeking confirmation through -- from this witness of things that eyewitness -- are factual evidence. This witness is an expert, Mr. Milovancevic. He has come here to give expert evidence. Will you please be relevant and stay within the purpose of this witness's testimony. You're seeking this witness's confirmation of a statement made in court by a Prosecutor. That statement by a Prosecutor is a mere allegation. The Prosecutor still has to call a witness to testify on those -- on those allegations. This witness was not an eyewitness in that trial either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in his report, on page of 6 -- 68 in B/C/S version and on page 12 of the English version, this witness speaks about the attack on Skabrnja, and he describes what he established based on his conversations with the survivors, and I'm merely asking whether what he established concurs with what Mr. Whiting said at the Babic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine. That's why I asked you my question. Does this concur with what you said where, what? Quote him exactly what he said so that he knows where to go and he can be able to answer you to say he does agree it, or he doesn't agree it. But if you just say what you wrote, and you're telling him what the Prosecutor said in court it's not very helpful, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On page 12 of the English version and page 668 of the B/C/S version in the last paragraph, you speak about Skabrnja and Nadin, and you say that: "It has been revealed that members of the JNA and Serbian paramilitary forces randomly chose villagers, the only criteria being that it was discovered" -- I am speeding and the interpreters are having a hard time. "It has been discovered that after entering the villages members of the JNA and Serbian paramilitary forces randomly chose villagers, the only criteria being their nationality, and killed them." And my question is whether this statement of yours concurs with what Mr. Whiting said at the Babic trial. Is that the case, Mr. Loncar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit, Your Honours, it is very difficult for me to follow the two things at the same time, and it's very difficult for me to see who said what. Let me consult my report first.
