utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is whether this part of your statement -- is this a part of your statement relative to Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is indeed relative to Skabrnja and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is Skabrnja, English page 12.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting spoke about that on page 76 in the transcript from the Babic trial. Page 76 of the transcript. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see Skabrnja anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Page 76, line 9. A second witness provides evidence about the attack by Serb forces on Skabrnja on the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian soldiers, including JNA soldiers and SAO Krajina soldiers, intentionally executed civilians during the attack, including elderly and women." And this is the exact same information that you provided in your report. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have my information that I received from the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the same page, page 76 of the transcript, Mr. Whiting, in lines 13 and 14, speaks about a crime in Bruska, in Bruska and about the Krajina milicija that came to the village of Bruska on the 21st of December, 1991 and massacred 10 civilians. On page 669 in the B/C/S version, I believe that it is on page 12 in the English version, you also speak about Bruska, and you speak about persons coming to the door, introducing themselves as members of the Martic milicija, and killed people there. Is that what it says in your report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I have been able to get my bearings between one paper and the other, which is very confusing Your Honours -- hold on just a moment. Let's me see. The village -- yes. Yes. This is from a statement of the survivors, of the eyewitnesses of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And let's finish with this page 76 before the break. I'm sorry, we still have another 15 minutes to go. The second witness quoted on this page by the Prosecutor Whiting speaks about Poljanak and how civilians were executed there. And finally in lines 21 and 22, the Prosecutor speaks about a witness who provides evidence about the arrest by Martic's milicija and his detention in the old hospital in Knin. Were you aware of these events? Did you hear about these events from the victims?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Still, I have to offer my apologies to the Trial Chamber, because I find it quite difficult. And if I may ask you to clarify your question first before I try and answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is what Mr. Whiting is stating here before the case against Milan Babic the same sort of evidence you received in your work with witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of just a cursory glance of this -- well, I find it quite difficult to juggle between the two papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I thank you for your answer, and I do agree with you that it is a bit difficult to follow. On page 77 of the transcript dating back to 2004, Mr. Whiting says that the Prosecution and Defence invited a joint witness where the name of Dr. Mladen Loncar is mentioned - that's on page 77 in lines 13 and 14 - who is a psychiatrist with expertise in dealing with victims of war or war crimes and who will testify about the effects on the victims of the crimes in Croatia that occurred in this case. Is that the task you were given in giving your expertise in the Babic case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been telling you all this time, Your Honour, that my task was to talk about the health impact on victims of these crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Milovancevic please repeat the references to the page numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you're being asked to repeat the reference to the page number because the interpreters have lost it or they didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Page 79 of the transcript, lines 14 and 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting describes your role as an expert witness in the following way: "Mr. Mladen Loncar will testify not only about the effects of the crimes on the victims but also about the positive effects from the accused's guilty plea and his acknowledgement of responsibility." Was that your task as well, Mr. Loncar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my task to say what sort of an effect Mr. Babic's guilty plea would have on both sides, on both ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have just established what your task was in developing this expert report. Could we please look at page 116 of the transcript? At the very top of page 116, when the Prosecutor completed his cross-examination -- Mr. Loncar, you have the page numeration there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to have several copies of the same page. That's why I'm confused. You said 116?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Lines 5 and 6. In response to the question put by the Presiding Judge whether there was any need for the Defence to cross-examine Dr. Loncar, the Defence counsel for Mr. Babic answered that there were no questions from the Defence side. Therefore, Mr. Mueller did not put any questions to you. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was one question. That's why I said that I thought I was examined by Mr. Mueller. It was a very brief one, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But in principle, there was no cross-examination, was there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I can't really judge to what extent one has to be examined to be considered as -- for that to be considered as cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you wish to call into doubt the text that you have before you on page 111, lines 5, 6, where Mr. Mueller says that there are no questions from the Defence side?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I simply don't remember anymore. There was discussion. Now, whether that was an actual discussion or a question-answer situation, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For the guidance of the witness, is it possible that you might be referring to the question that you were asked by the Judge? Because I see according to the transcript that Judge El Mahdi asked the question: "Doctor, I would like to ask you --" well, first of all, Judge Orie said: "Judge El Mahdi has one more question for you." That's the one question that came from Judge El Mahdi. Could you be confusing the question from Judge El Mahdi as a question from the Defence? Did you hear my question, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I apologise. I thought the question was put to the Defence. Yes, that's quite possible, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you see that, Mr. Milovancevic, that Dr. -- I beg your pardon, Judge El Mahdi asked one question to the witness? I don't know whether that's the one question he's referring to when he says he was cross-examined by the asking of one question. But your opposite number is on her feet. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Looking further along on the transcript, I don't know if my learned friend intended to go this far, but at page 123 there is a question by counsel Mr. Fogelnest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And who was Mr. Fogelnest?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Defence counsel for Mr. Babic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be of assistance? This was part of re-examination in view of the fact that the Defence stated that it had no questions during cross-examination, next followed questions from the Bench, and then the Defence counsel stood up for re-examination, but that cannot be considered as cross-examination. Perhaps that's what the witness was referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is true, but this witness is not going to know the distinction between all those things. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I was actually going to say that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see, all he will remember is that a lawyer stood up on the opposite side and asked me questions. What stage of the trial that is he may not be able to tell. Be that as it may, I think everybody in court here does accept that there was no cross-examination, that questions were asked arising from questions asked by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have finished with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will now put to you some questions concerning your expert report. We have already mentioned pages 2 and 3 where the lines could be found concerning the method of taking statements, which had several goals. And then -- this was at page 656. And then the next chapter is entitled "The victims of incarceration," which in the English version can be found on page 3. Witness, have you found the page?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the introduction itself, you say that: "From a moral and humanistic aspect, camps have always been places of the greatest devaluation of people, therefore, they are also the greatest systematic degradations of the code of ethics." I'm interested in the following: Is this your position vis-a-vis victims who were held in camps regardless of their ethnicity and regardless of the whereabouts of these camps? Is this a universal characteristic shared by all victims?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I stated here, it does not imply that not all the victims are the same whatever their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the next page, in the B/C/S it's page 657 and in the English version that's page 3, and I'm referring to the second paragraph from the bottom where you say: "Between 650 and 700 non-Serbs were incarcerated in Knin camps." Have you found that part of the text?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 39 of the indictment against Mr. Martic, the allegations by the OTP include the following facilities, and I will now quote the indictment allegations. Short-term and long-term detention facilities are mentioned. That's at paragraph 39 of the indictment. And as such the detention centres include the Knin prison run by the JNA, which had about 150 detainees. That's under (a). And under (b), the old hospital in Knin, which as the indictment alleges was run by Martic's police and had about 120 detainees. Under (c) of paragraph 39 of the indictment lists the police station at Titova Korenica which had 10 detainees. Under (d) of the same paragraph, the police station at Bosanska Kostajnica is alleged with 8 -- 10 -- 8 to 10 detainees. Under (e), the police station at Bosanski Novi with 50 detainees. And lastly, under (f), the shoe factory Sloga at Prnjavor with 180 detainees. I put this to you in order to demonstrate one fact. When you sum up all of the figures in the indictment, you arrive at about 500 people in all. In this expert report of yours, you give the figure of 650 and -- to 700 persons in the Knin camps. What was the basis for this figure of yours?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated yesterday, during the period when I had contacts with people who were in the area in the period between 1991 and 1995 and from conversations with them, I arrived at this approximate figure of 650 to 700 persons. Another explanation for this figure is that the victims themselves stated that the victims included not only citizens of Croatia but also of Bosnia and Herzegovina, from the Bihac area. I did not state all these details here, but I'm simply explaining how I arrive at the figure here. One part of the victims were allegedly exchanged to Kupres. That's what I heard from the stories of those who were in these facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But this figure is not consistent with what the Prosecutor alleges, but I believe we shall deal with this after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it's the time now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will deal with that, and just be thinking during the break whether that question will be relevant, Mr. Milovancevic. This witness is an expert witness. His figures are estimates which have nothing to do with the case. It's the effects of the trauma. Just think about that. Court adjourned. We will come back at a quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, before the break we stopped with the third chapter, the victims of detention and its general characteristics and how it affects people.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your expert report on page 659 in B/C/S and page 4 of the English version, in the last paragraph you dealt with the most common psychological impairments, and you say that there is anxiety. And the third impairment is depressive reactions and similar symptoms. With this regard I don't have any questions, because I assume that this is a general picture of all the people who have ever been detained in the institutions of the sort described in this report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the English version, page 6 of your report, and in B/C/S on page 660, this is where the fourth chapter starts, and this is where you speak about the victims of displacement and victims whose homes were destroyed and who lost everything. In this paragraph, you say that those are refugees and displaced persons who experienced the so-called dislocation stress which is one of the most difficult or gravest stresses for a human being, and this is something that every human being finds very difficult to deal with as a change that affects a human being. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the Secretary-General of the United Nations' report, it says that towards the end of 1991 in the territory of the former Yugoslavia there were 500.000 refugees and displaced persons. Are you aware of that information?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the fact that at one point in time in the territory, and I don't know when that was, in the territory of Croatia alone there were between 400 and 500.000 refugees and displaced persons. So I wouldn't go into your information. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Regardless of the figures, the conclusions that you offer in your report with regard to the so-called dislocation stress apply to all these people.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On page 661 of your report in the B/C/S version, and in the English version this is on page 6, paragraph 3, you say that from the territory of SAO Krajina -- I apologise. I started talking without a mic. On the English page 6 of your report, and on page 661 of the B/C/S, you say that tens of thousands of Croats and non-Serbs were displaced or fled from the so-called Krajina SAO. Practically the entire non-Serb population was deported, forcefully removed or killed. There was intentional destruction of homes, private property, public and cultural institutions, cultural monuments and sacral buildings of the Croatian and other non-Serbian population, especially in Dubica, Cerovljani, Bacin, Saborsko, Poljanak, Lipovaca, and the hamlets of Vaganac, Skabrnja, Nadin, and Bruska in Krajina SAO. Did you notice that this paragraph in your expert report is almost identical of paragraph 23(j) in the indictment against Mr. Martic? Is this your finding or is this something that you copied from the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my authentic finding that I drafted in order to describe the dramatic experience of this group, and this experience assumed the proportions of an epidemic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Based on your conversations with the certain numbers of victims, you were able to establish that several tens of thousands, as you say, of Croats and non-Serbs, or practically the entire non-Serbian population was deported, forcefully removed or killed. And also that their property was intentionally destroyed. And this is what you could establish based on your conversations with the victims.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may repeat, deported, forcefully removed -- or forcibly removed or killed, and this is the exact wording in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will read to you paragraph 23 of the indictment, which under item (e) says: "Deportations or forcible removal of tens of thousands of Croatian and other non-Serb civilians," and under item (j), it says, and that is something that you also say in your paragraph, "intentional destruction of residential buildings, private and public property, cultural institutions, cultural monuments, and sacral buildings of the Croatian, Muslim, and other non-Serb population, especially in Dubica, Cerovljani, Bacin, Saborsko ..." Let me not repeat the names of the villages that you mention in your report. Did you take that text over from the indictment? Did you take this over from Mr. Whiting or did he take this over from you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't take this anything from anybody. And as you were reading the text of the indictment, I cannot say that the two are identical. They are not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you say that they're almost 100 per cent identical, the two texts?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your view, they're not identical?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they're not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I do hate to interrupt you, but what further evidential value do the answers have other than what is already contained in the report? Are these points which you're attempting to make not better made in the course of an address by way of a comparison of the two documents whilst you will have the opportunity at a later stage to bring this to the attention of the Court? Is it suitable for cross-examination in this way?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am agreeable with your suggestion entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the same page, which is pages 6 and 7 of the English version, you explain the stages in the stress-building that the refugees have to go through. Since you have providing a great detail in that description, at this moment I will not asking any questions about that part of your report. I'm interested in your allegation on page 7, which is 662 in the B/C/S version, and the English page 7, where you say: "A majority of the displaced persons left their homes during the armed conflict. Many were forced to leave their homes because of physical abuse or direct endangerment of their lives."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What paragraph must we look at on page 7, and where in --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell you in a second, Your Honours. This is the last paragraph on page 7, Your Honours, below items 1, 3, 4 [as interpreted]. The last paragraph on page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This information is it based on your conversations with the victims. Is that correct, Mr. Loncar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On pages 7 and 8 of the English and page 663 of the B/C/S version, you speak about these symptoms that the displaced persons experience.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that they fall under the international classification 10 and that they occur as a consequence of an acute stress or trauma, and this is a general characteristic of all the people that went through such an experience. Is that correct, Mr. Loncar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my sample this was absolutely the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 664 of the B/C/S version, and in English this is on page 9, you speak about the municipality of Hrvatska Dubica, and you explain its make-up as consisting of the following places: Dubica, Bacin, Slavinja, Zivaja, and Cerovljani. Slavinja and Zivaja are Serbian villages, villages with a majority Serbian population. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you were talking about the effects of persecution, you, I suppose, had in mind their lot, the lot of these villages.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not my intention to deal with villages geographically but primarily with traumatised people, and within that -- that context I wanted to see what had happened to certain groups, to the groups of the people with whom I had had contact during the war, with whom I had spoken during the war. And initially I wanted to see what caused their possible health complaints and problems. Hence the short introduction, just as an illustration as to what I'm going to say next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you mentioned the village of Bacin and the village of Cerovljani in the same paragraph, as well as the village of Pregore, you're talking about the consequences of the events that these people had been through. Do you deal with them as the victims of persecution or the victims of something else, some other sort of victims?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I mention these villages and the entire paragraph on page 660, under IV, I'm talking about the victims of deportation whose homes were destroyed. I'm talking about displaced persons who -- whose homes were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned the villages of Bacin, Cerovljani and Dubica, are you aware of the fact that yesterday we had a witness who explained that the population was not expelled from those villages, that they went from the village on the 13th and 14th of September 1991 pursuant to the HDZ's and Crisis Staff instruction, and that what happened in Bacin with the graveyard, that happened in October 1991. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you said that somebody from the HDZ sent them away. I don't know that. I'm not aware of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, we've had other witnesses here who spoke about a person called Matilja from Hrvatska Kostajnica and his implementation of Tudjman's order. Did you not hear of that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Two paragraphs below the one that we were looking at just now you mention the village of Cerovljani, and you spoke about the persecution of some 180 Croats. There was a Prosecution witness here who told us that the population had left the village before the conflict, in the first half of September, and if I put it to you this way, would you still say that this was a case of persecution?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I was writing this, I used a general wording, and it was not my intention to legally define their position. What I was interested in as a doctor who worked with that group of displaced persons is the fact that they could not go home. They could not return to their homes, that they had problems as a result of that, and that their homes had been destroyed. And what I found important and what I wrote about was what health complaints prevailed in this group of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Loncar. When you mentioned these villages, Bacin, Dubica, and Cerovljani, you mention on the following page, which is the English page 10, and in B/C/S this is page 665, the penultimate paragraph, you say that about 95 per cent of the displaced persons returned to that area. Do you know what happened to the Serbs from this area? Did they ever return?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the information that was not broken down according to ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On page 466 -- or 666 in the upper right corner, and we're talking about relatives, victims, relatives of those who were killed. In the first paragraph -- have you been able to locate this, Mr. Loncar? In the first paragraph here you're talking about what the relatives of the victims experienced, and you talk about their general and specific experiences. On the following page marked as 667 in B/C/S, and on page 11 of the English version, in the penultimate paragraph -- did you find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says here that: "From the beginning of August 1991 to the end of February 1992 Serbian forces in the so-called Krajina SAO or RSK consisted of the JNA, the local Serbian TO and TO units from Serbia and Montenegro, as well as local police units and police units of the Serbian MUP and Serbian paramilitary units. They attacked and took control in towns and villages. After taking control, they established a government that intentionally displaced the Croatian and non-Serb population and drove them out of these areas. These expulsions were based on political, natural and religious factors." Are you aware of the fact that this text is identical to -- with paragraph 22 of the indictment and 23 of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that the existence of an identical text is the result of your work rather than of using the indictment of the -- itself? Is that the way I am supposed to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. Can the Defence repeat the question? What is identical to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have before me the text of the indictment and what you wrote about what happened between August and so on and so forth, and what follows is the verbatim part of the indictment, absolutely identical to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question? Your Honours, can you help me? Can you ask the Defence counsel to tell me what the question is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How do you account for the fact that one part of your text is identical to one part of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to answer by providing you two answers. First of all, I'm not aware of that; and secondly, this is not important. This is just an illustration. Every time I described the health problems, I introduced that by some illustrations in order to establish that introduction with the health problems that I found important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, you find irrelevant the fact that the general climate of persecutions, which allegedly exist in a given area, you analyse in a piece of text which is practically identical to the text in the indictment and that is the piece of text you place in the context of your expert report. Can this piece of text with the position expressed therein, can it not have an impact on your expert report overall?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I based my expert report on the stories told by hundreds of victims who had gone through their experiences on the basis of their ethnicity and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Except for two or three examples, I did not see tens or hundreds and let alone tens of thousands of testimonials that you speak of which would account for the displacement of these people. You state that you base your report on about 100 testimonials.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on a bit more than that, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: However, you put parts of the indictment in your expert report.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the indictment itself does not speak of the health condition of these people, and I wouldn't have any point in taking that text. The victims told me how they felt, and medically speaking they are entitled to their own subjective opinion as to what their experiences were like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: A bit below the text we just looked at we have another paragraph which is at page 668 in the B/C/S, and that's the paragraph starting on page 11 and continuing on to page 12 in the English. You state: "That is how the following crimes occurred: In October 1991 in Hrvatska Kostajnica municipality, Serbian forces consisting of the JNA, the local Serb TO, and Martic's police captured 53 civilians in Dubica village and incarcerated them at the village fire station. On the 21st of October, 1991, members of the Serb forces took the 43 captured Croats to an area near the village of Bacin where they brought over 13 more non-Serb civilians from Bacin and Cerovljani and there they killed these 56 people. At the same time, Serb forces took 30 more civilians from Bacin and 24 civilians from Dubica and Cerovljani villages to an unknown location and killed them." This is what you write in your report.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That is the quotation from your report. I find quite telling the fact that this text is identical to the text that can be found in paragraph 26 of the indictment. Is this the sort of text you arrived at based on the testimonials of the victims?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, yes, from the victims I listened to who told me their experiences and told me how they were taken over and detained at the local fire department. That is literally the statement of victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Two paragraphs down from the text we looked at on page 12 you speak of Saborsko. Next you speak of Lipovaca and Vukovici. Interestingly, the text concerning Saborsko, Lipovaca and Vukovici is identical to the one to be found in the indictment; paragraph 30 for Saborsko and paragraphs 28 and 29 for Lipovaca and Vukovici. Do you believe this to be a coincidence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information I drew upon was the information I received from victims, and this can be double-checked. I can be called again to testify on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You state that at least 31 persons were killed in Saborsko. In the indictment there's the figure of 20. You state that seven civilians were killed in Lipovaca, and the indictment it is said that eight of them were killed. You state that 10 civilians were killed in Vukovici, whereas the indictment alleges that 9 of them were killed. And that's the only difference. But all of the information contained here is the result of your work, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The figures which are the indicators of the subject are the ones that I arrived at from victims, and they are in fact just the way of introducing the topic of the health condition of these workers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Milovancevic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you this question, Mr. Loncar, is that I, as a Defence counsel, find it interesting that you draw upon the text which is identical to that of the indictment in order to illustrate the situation on the ground. On page 668, the last sentence of the last paragraph, which is at page 12 in the English version, you state the following: "During the month of November of 1991, the Serb forces entered Skabrnja and they went from house to house killing 38 non-Serb civilians in their homes and out in the street. And in the period between 18 November 1991 and February 1992, the remainder of the infirm civilians in Skabrnja were killed." What I find interesting in this text is that it seems to have been copied from paragraph 31 of the indictment. You are not aware of any such coincidence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not. Your Honours, allow me to explain this further. I happen to have visited Skabrnja a month ago, and I can tell you that the figures are relevant because they can be read out from the memorials that were raised there, erected there, in the memory of these victims. Unfortunately, these same figures were etched in marble there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also state that 56 remaining infirm civilians were killed in Skabrnja, whereas the Prosecutor speaks of 26 civilians killed. How did you arrive at the figures here?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the methodology was the same. It was the information conveyed to me by victims who related their experience. And again I repeat this was simply an introduction to what was to follow, which was the impact of these events on the health of this particular group of victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you become a fact witness by drawing upon the facts on the ground? Because you seem to be testifying on a whole lot of facts in your expert report. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not share your view. These facts serve only as an illustration to point to the cause and effect link between the events and the problems experienced by these victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On page 14 of the English version, and in the B/C/S that's page 671 of your report -- have you found that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: There's chapter 6, "Victims - relatives of missing persons." There you are referring to the period during which most of the persons went missing.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also go on to explain how the fact that family members have persons missing influences their own health condition, and that's the way in which normally a person reacts to such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I can say that that's correct, but that's the information that I was able to arrive at on the basis of the group of victims I analysed. I cannot say for a fact that a different group of victims would not have reacted differently. Of course, the cultural background also comes into play. But generally speaking, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On page 673, which in the English version can be found at page 16, Your Honours, paragraph 3, you speak of the impossibility for the family whose member went missing to return to the location where the person was last seen because it re-traumatises them. You draw the following conclusion from there: That this kind of situation additionally enhances the lack of confidence vis-a-vis members of Serb ethnicity which makes any form of reconciliation difficult. Which members of Serb ethnicity are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the areas where such persons looking after missing persons could not feel safe in going back to. And these are some parts of the Republic of Croatia, on the border between Croatia and Serbia. These are persons who actually follow clues or hints telling them that this is where their missing family members could be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You go on to say that this lack of trust on the part of Croats vis-a-vis Serbs living in the areas that you just mentioned exists because they, the victims, believe that persons of Serb ethnicity who were staying in the area where their family members went missing during the war know what happened to these missing members of their family but do not wish to speak about it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the view of these relatives of the victims, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your conclusion, chapter 7, English page 17, 674 is the B/C/S page, you're talking about the effect of the confession on the -- on the victims. And at the very end of this second paragraph below the title, which is on English 17, last page -- last paragraph, and in B/C/S this is 675, you say that at the -- Mr. Babic's confession conveys a message that it is not the person that has to be hated but the sin committed by the person. Mr. Babic's confession in which he says that there is a person rather than a nation in every crime committed and that the person commits the crime hiding behind the nation and the ideology, and this has helped victims to see the crimes not through the prism of a nation but through the person who committed them. Does it apply not only to Mr. Babic but also to every other such perpetrator of a crime?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, could you please be more succinct. Are you referring to Mr. Babic's confession or something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I quoted a very long part of your own text. When you say that Mr. Babic's confession shows that there is a person, not a nation behind every crime and that it helps victims to see the crimes not through the prism of a nation but through the prism of a person who committed them, this position of yours the result of a principle according to which every perpetrator of every crime has a name?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that in the course of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the next chapter you speak about the effect of Babic's confession on the Croatian population, and below that we see the effect of the confession on the Serbian population. You explain that only one's admission of guilt for the crimes committed allows for the lifting of responsibility from the whole nation. And then you continue to say when this is done by a leader, this may be a relief for his subordinates who have followed his orders, and perhaps they will be able to assume their personal responsibility and to allow the Serbian people to turn towards the future. What subordinates did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we speak about subordinates, I'm talking about the hierarchy, and we have to make two distinctions here. In these areas, leadership, regardless of the ethnic background, is made equal with the national affiliation. That's why I said that national affiliation has to be dissociated from the perpetrator of a crime. The perpetrators of crimes will often say that they are committing crimes with a cause, the cause being a national interest, although in reality this is not true. For that reason, a commission -- a confession removes this prejudice that all the crimes of that kind are committed for a nation. And crimes are often perceived by victims as crimes committed by one nation against another. It is our task and our job to individualise, to personalise the perpetrators of a crime which may be of a certain ethnic background, but that doesn't mean that this ethnic group is a group of criminals. That doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I agree with that completely, but I'm interested in the rest of your sentence or the paragraph in which you say that the assumption of individual responsibility for the acts committed will enable the Serbian people to turn to the future and take on a level of compassion which will allow their crimes to be forgiven. Who is -- who is it who is supposed to forgive the Serbian people in order for them to be able to continue their life?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, they are psychological categories, not legal categories. In other words, what happened in the psychology of an ethnic group, either one or the other. As we both know, it often happens that in a nation which results from a lack of caution or for some other reasons, when the perpetrator is a Serb, all of a sudden there is an identification process with the Serbian nation. In order to avoid that, because this is wrong, if the true perpetrator of a crime is found, is identified, then this psychological dimension that is hanging in the air in the territory of the former Yugoslavia is automatically removed. It disappears. And this is the context into which you have to put this sentence. This will allow our people to turn to the future rather than to reflect on the legacies of the crimes committed by groups or individuals in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you're talking about Mr. Babic's confession, I would like to ask you whether you ever spoke to Mr. Babic to talk about that, or did you analyse his personality?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Based on your report and based on Prosecutor's word, Mr. Babic was sentenced to 13 words -- to 13 years, not to 11, as was proposed, and the -- his Defence counsel did not cross-examine you. At that moment, he was an accused who was staying in a private house, not in the Detention Unit, but we are going to ask Mr. Whiting and Mrs. Vesna [phoen] about that when our case comes. I would like to know whether the announcement of suicide of Mr. Babic after all this was the result of failed expectations or some other impairments? Do you have any idea of the health of Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in the Babic case that I did not have any insight into his health condition, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the report of the committee that investigated his death, it -- it says that he spoke to his family and that he told them that it was his impression that he was being abused or ill-used by the Prosecution. It is also known that when he testified in the Martic case the OTP was in the process of dealing with the -- his family situation, the situation of his family and their whereabouts. Would you say that this was --

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- relevant and the situation of his family could have had an impact on Mr. Babic and what he did?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. There is an objection be raised. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the OTP was not dealing with his family. That was the province of the registry. This is an inaccurate statement on the part of my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you have any response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the report of the so-called Parker's committee, it says that Mr. Babic was under a great deal of stress as a result of the fact that during his testimony the situation and status of his family was being dealt with. The question of the status of his family and the place where he would serve his sentence was part of the agreement with the OTP at the time when Mr. Babic struck the deal with OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I'll ask you to please stay focused yourself. The objection is simply this: That the OTP was not dealing with Mr. Babic's family, that that was the province of the Registry. Now, you either accept that or you dispute that. Just answer to that and just don't tell us a lot of history. There is just one little point that is being made. Deal with that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with that, Your Honour. Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you always agree after going all over the show? Okay. Just deal with that point then. Was it the province of the Registry, or was it the province of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree that this is and different subject, but my question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no. Don't go to your question, Mr. Milovancevic. Just respond to the objection, please. Was it the province of the Registry, or was it the province of the OTP? I don't want to circumvent and repeat your question before you've dealt with the objection. Deal with the objection and let's get over it, then you can ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I find it absolutely relevant, Your Honour, because this was happening at the moment when the OTP was examining Babic in the Martic case, and he complained to his family that he felt abused. And coincidentally the status of his family was being dealt with, and this all hangs like a sword above his head. And just by pure accident the guy killed himself at the moment. I'm asking the psychiatrist whether such a situation could have an impact on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I rule out of order the whole statement that you have made right now. You have not answered my question. My question to you is: Was his family being dealt with by the OTP or was it dealt with by the Registry? Now stop going behind the objection, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I understand. I understand. I read the text of the so-called Parker's commission, and I understood it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you are not answering my question. I disallow you from further talking on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, I fully believe that it was the OTP who was dealing with that. Thank you, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You either believe or you have facts to state that on. If it's a belief on and we are having a statement that it has been stated by the OTP, they said clearly that they didn't deal with his family. Now, you go check your beliefs, and when you have checked them you can come to court with your questions, but for now the Court forbids you from asking questions on that point, and the objection is upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, we have come almost to the end of the cross-examination. In your expert report, at the very end of this report -- I apologise. Just bear with me for a moment and I will give you the page indication. When you speak -- and this is on page 675 in B/C/S and page 18 in the English version. And when you speak about the effect of the confession on the Serbian population, you are quoting testimonial of an 11-year-old girl about how she perceived the situation. And you continue to say that this was a case, and you say that this is a case, and it's a child from Skabrnja whose parents and grandparents were killed. She writes in a school composition: "It all happened very quickly. Black birds of prey set off, towards the sun, switched it off and in one day I lost my father, grandmother, and both my grandfathers." At the end of that quotation you go on to say: "Who is it who spilled the black colour of misfortune of my childhood, and is this how it should have happened?" And this is the statement of the child from Skabrnja. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a school composition that the child wrote at school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that this paint, the black paint of unhappiness all over her childhood, the childhood of this child and all the other childhood [as interpreted], was spilled by the person who issued an order to form a -- the Skabrnja battalion that will attack the regular JNA forces in that area and who had turned the village into a fortress?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this short poem or a composition written by a child was quoted by me for the reason that it contains suffering, the loss that the child had experienced, and because of the ending. I was very partial to the ending where she says that the child -- the child says that the world is merciless. In her imagination, in her fairy tale she wants everything to be nicer and good to over -- to always win over the evil, and because of that I included this into my report. This is universal. The good always win over -- win over evil. We have a saying in our -- in my language that says after rain, sun, but I like this better. And this is why I included it after I had come into contact with that child. When I had read that composition, I realised that the child had problems and that she is sending universal messages, and this is the essence of that story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can this sort of question be also addressed to the president of Croatia, Tudjman, who in 1991 stated that there would have been no war had Croatia not wanted it? And that was the -- in 1992 the anniversary of Croatia's secession. Is that the sort of thing that should also be addressed to him?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not investigate into the causes of these events. I merely looked at the consequences. And I repeat that I chose this because of the universal message contained there, that the good should always win over the evil.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have completed my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like a moment to confer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: No further questions from the Prosecution of this witness, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Valabhji. Judge. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Are either post-traumatic stress disorder or acute stress disorder permanent state and conditions in respect of victims?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is what the situation is like: Acute stress reaction to torture, which is something that was shown in our area, is something that lasts from six months to one year at the most. This is an acute disorder which is limited in duration, whereas the post-traumatic stress disorder with all the symptoms inherent to it can also have an acute stage which is normally quite short and falls within this time frame of six months to one year where you find these symptoms. However, its permanent effect can last for life in some victims and in others it may disappear. It depends on the person's disposition, predilection. It depends on how strong the person is. It depends also on the social, economic, and other conditions and the sort of support the person receives. If there is no re-traumatisation in the person, then there is a likelihood that the disorder and its symptoms will disappear. I also wish to say that the post-traumatic stress disorder can have its mild forms, moderate forms, up to the very serious and grave forms. This is also something that will affect the prognosis of the disorder and its duration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The victims who form the subject matter of your report, are you still in touch with them clinically?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do work with victims a great deal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm speaking of the ones who form the subject matter of your report, who you interviewed for the basis of your report.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am in touch with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Can you speak to the percentage of recovery, of complete recovery? Is it possible?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we frequently say in psychiatry is that if the -- in the case of the post-traumatic stress disorder, this is the sort of recovery -- or the sort of criteria we use to establish whether there is any recovery. This is, first of all, criterion A under DSM-IV, which is the American classification, and then we have the other, MKB-10, which is the requirement that the person has had to go through an extreme trauma that placed her life in danger or that it involved such an amount of fear of such intensity that it caused a threat to the person's life. Such reactions normally remain registered in our engrams, that is to say in the persons who went through the experience. However, if they have symptoms from the third, fourth, and fifth categories, then we can easily take them through the treatment procedure to deal with their flashbacks, re-traumatisations and so on. The second group of symptoms are hyper-sensitivity, sleeplessness, insomnia, acting out reactions, decreased emotional control, and prominent expression of emotions. The third group of symptoms include the so-called symptoms of evasion which associate the person or remind the person of the trauma. These can normally be easily controlled either through psychiatric therapy or through medicines. We did not deal with permanent memories, the permanent scars, but we can treat these groups of symptoms I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: All right. Now, you have been asked many questions in cross-examination concerning the contents of your report as against the contents of sections of the indictment. Had you seen the indictment at the time that you prepared your report? Had you perused it and read it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, on the internet. However, I was looking at the indictment against Mr. Babic. I'm not aware of the indictment against Mr. Babic -- Martic. I don't believe that I have perused it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I was speaking concerning the indictment in this case, in this case against the accused Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that the indictment can be found on the internet, but I did not read it. I saw it, but I did not read it. I'm not privy to the details therefore. I really did not read it, because I was told to deal with the health condition and so on and so forth. So I did not think it necessary to look into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Had you discussed with the OTP the contents of the indictment before or at the time that you were compiling your report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, are you referring to the indictment against Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The indictment against Mr. Martic which I understood to be the indictment than learned counsel for the Defence was referring to when he cross-examined you.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not discussed anything in particular of that sort with the Prosecution save for the matters upon which I was called to come here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: In the entire contents of your report as it relates to the areas in the indictment that counsel referred you to would be based on your clinical experience with the victims? Is that a fact or is it not so?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're talking about the impact on the health of the victims, these were the findings based on my work with victims. I can explain in terms of the fact that I did not include in my report all the information concerning the health of these victims. If the Trial Chamber is interested, I can tell you which these are. I did mention them. I outlined them, but I did not consider it necessary to go into that great a detail as I was asked to produce a report covering some 15 to 20 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Doctor, can I -- are you able to explain to us how you came into contact with your interviewees for purposes of this report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information on the health condition of these victims as I explained in the introductory part of my report, and there has been some confusion regarding that in my testimony, I arrived at on the basis of the methodology that I also used in drafting my report. I stated that I collected the information from victims of whom I took statements, testimonials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me -- let me try to rephrase my question. How did you come into initial contact with each victim that you interviewed?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were two main ways in which these persons were contacted. Most often we would go to refugee centres or centres holding displaced persons where we first of all wanted to inquire as to how we could be of assistance to them. This was normally the first contact. The second type of contact was with the so-called inmates, camp inmates, former camp inmates, and we would get in touch with them in the centres where they would put up -- where they were put up after having been exchanged. We also discussed with them ways of assisting them. We also collected different information from refugees and displaced persons as well as former detainees, and on the basis of that information we got in touch with their families and tried to assist them anyway we could. We would also get in touch with them in the following way: In the case of victims of sexual abuse, for instance, women, we would get in touch with the social institutions under whose care these women were, and that was how we would get in touch with them and talk to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it -- do I understand you to be saying that victims of sexual abuse you sought out?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them, yes, whereas a smaller number of them approached us in search of assistance. As for the victims of sexual abuse, if I may be allowed to proceed, Your Honour, just a few more remarks. The most important thing was to gain their trust and to have more than one contact with them in order for us to become closer to the person, win their trust, and then by talking to the persons we would get an insight into their trauma. We would then proceed to treat such victims in the best way we knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In other words, they did not up front, voluntarily -- let me rephrase. They did not volunteer up front the fact of their sexual abuse. You had to gain their confidence and trust before they could volunteer this information.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You were shown pictures this afternoon on the ELMO. I'm not quite sure -- I just wanted to find out how -- you were asked about the ethnicity of some of the people. How do you recognise -- I beg your pardon. How do you determine the ethnicity of a person by looking on a picture on the ELMO there? You might as well tell me also how you determine where the person comes from by the same process.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, you are absolutely right. When I said earlier today and "recognised" these bodies, it was just my assumption because those people had been brought from the village of Doljani, and the photos were taken by a friend of mine, a doctor, and that's why I provided the answer that I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, these people whose pictures you were being shown today, were they alive? Have you seen them in life, or when you saw them, if you did see them at all, were they already dead?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were dead already, Your Honour, at the moment when I saw the photos, that is. And the fellow villagers who were displaced from the village recognised them on those photos, and there was also subsequent identification of the bodies with the assistance of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So in fact, the people you saw -- that we saw this afternoon on the pictures here were never the subject of your report or your interviews. You didn't interview them. They were corpses when you first saw their pictures.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never got in contact with them because I never saw them alive. That's what I'm saying. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You had seen these photographs before today, had you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. A colleague of mine took these photos, and I did see them before. That's why I found it easy to recognise them, although I had not seen them in a long time before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In other words, when you characterised them in terms of ethnicity and residence, you did so on what you were told by other people? You had no independent knowledge of that? Or, rather, let me put it this way: It's not -- it's not information that you got from an interview with these people?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It was the second-hand knowledge based on the information from the survivors. I repeat, the persons that we saw on those photos earlier today, I never spoke to them when they were alive, never spoke to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you can just give me a moment. I'm sorry, I'm not finding what I'm looking for. The numbering is different. Thank you very much. That concludes the questions from -- sorry, I think Judge Nosworthy has a question to ask just before I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Doctor, you're in the peculiar position of having been a victim of certain experiences as well as an expert who has produced a report and given findings. Could you tell the Trial Chamber whether your personal experience affected or impacted in any way in the compilation of your report, in any process at all in relation to your report, and how, if at all, you were able to distinguish between the personal self and your professional self in terms of your experiences for the purposes of the preparation and settling of your report.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll try to answer your several questions, and I'll start with an illustration. In this case, I did not touch upon the part of the work that was not relevant for this case, because this was my instruction, to stick to the subject. I spoke about all victims in a book that was published in Zagreb, regardless of their ethnicity and who the perpetrators of the crimes were. And I also speak about the victims on the Croatian side, the Serb side, on all the sides. Let me try and answer your question more directly, Your Honour. My experience that I went through has helped me to supplement my education and to experience the universality of the victim and to understand fully that the victims cannot be segregated on no basis, and also I found confirmation that a criminal cannot hide behind their nationality. For that reason, I believe I have not had any problems with my dual status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge Hoepfel also has yet another question to ask, and I have found what I wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, could you in addition to what you just explained to Judge Nosworthy make a temporal relation between the time of your personal experience and the time when you prepared the report? Just an overall temporal structure, a time line.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the two experiences coincide in a way. What I went through helped me to understand what the cause is, and when I gained my education in -- in psychiatry, I could understand everything better, and this is the context in which I would put my report. One was history, and these are the consequences that I've described herein, and my personal experience has helped me in the way that the victims found it easier to believe me and trust me. They empathised with me, and they could sense that I understood them better than others. It is a very common occurrence, not only in my case, and that is that victims perceive a certain number of experts in whom they find more empathy for their suffering and their problems. This is at least what the victims experience, which doesn't necessarily mean there is a difference in the quality and the qualification of the doctor that is treating them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Would you give an overall time structure for your personal experiences and the time of preparation of the report? You may have said that, but my memory may be weak, so please could you clarify that? Did we have a time? Can you give us the time when that happened and when you prepared your report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time difference is some 13, 14 years, if we're talking about the time difference. I was arrested in 1991, and the report was written two years ago. So we're talking about a time difference of some 13, 14 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge. If everybody can indulge me, please, let me go back to the question I was looking for. Sometime today you indicated that the 53 civilians in the village of Dubica who were detained in the local fire station -- you referred to those people, and then you said after making that reference, "This is what I found." I assumed when you said, "This is what I found," you mean the 53 civilians, and I want to find out where did you find them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where did you find them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me just clarify this. When we're working in this way, when we're talking to victims like I did, and yesterday more than today we were talking about statistics. This is not so much about scientific statistics. In my job, I'm not an investigator but the victim has this need to talk to me, and I have to listen through to them, and sometimes it happens that victims volunteer certain numbers, and then another victim gives me a different number which may differ by one or two. Since I'm not an investigator, I'm just a doctor who spoke to the survivors of certain events, I took these numbers, these figures, as a mere illustration and as a starting point for the traumatic experience that I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I probably didn't express myself clearly. My question is simply where did you find them? Did you find them in the fire station, or did you find them elsewhere? I'm not asking you about the numbers and what have you. I understand you're not an investigator. You're just a doctor -- not just a doctor. You are a doctor. But I understand that. What I want is know is where physically did you find these people when you made contact with them for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they were still displaced persons and refugees, and these people spoke to me about the victims, if this is what you're asking me, if I understand your question well. These people, refugees and displaced persons, spoke to me about those victims, and they gave me the figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see. You did not speak to the 53 civilians who were in the fire station. You spoke to those who knew about them.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It didn't look -- it didn't look like that on the record. Thank you so much. That concludes my questions. Any -- not that you may ask the questions, I just want to find out if you do have any questions arising from the Bench's questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour, but I just would like to note in relation to a question posed by Her Honour Judge Nosworthy that the Babic indictment is Exhibit 173 in evidence in this case, and there is, I believe, considerable overlap with the indictment in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Valabhji. Mr. Milovancevic, any -- do you have any questions arising? We have gone far beyond the time. I just want to establish so that I know what to say to the witness. Do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please bear with me for a minute. I have a very brief question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is the witness aware of the fact that both Babic and Martic are indicted for the same joint criminal enterprise and that the basis of the crime is the same in both indictments? So the temporal and geographical reference is the same.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in Mr. Babic's indictment Mr. Martic is referred to. He is mentioned. This is what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm sorry to have kept everybody beyond the time. I hope you can bear with us. We just wanted to finish with this witness so we can release him today. Doctor, this brings us to the ends of your testimony. We will not need you any further, but we want to say thank you very much for coming to testify in the matter. You are now excused. You may stand down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
